Name: number_representation_language_independence
Title: A Language-Independent Number Line: How LLMs Represent Quantity Beneath the Words
Short Hypothesis: We hypothesize that LLMs encode numerical magnitude on a low-dimensional, approximately continuous manifold (a 'number line') that is shared across number words, digit strings, and languages, and that the fidelity of this manifold predicts arithmetic and quantitative-reasoning accuracy. This tests whether an abstract, non-linguistic magnitude representation underlies quantitative intelligence, independent of the linguistic form (word 'seven', digit '7', or other-language equivalents). This is the ideal setting because number offers a clean, gradable concept to separate form from abstract content.
Related Work: Work on numeric representations shows helix/circular structure for arithmetic (e.g., 'Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Math', 2025) and Fourier features for addition (Nanda et al. style). Cross-notation and cross-lingual number handling is studied behaviorally. We unify these by testing a single shared magnitude manifold across notations and languages and causally linking manifold fidelity to reasoning accuracy, distinguishing abstract-magnitude representation from notation-specific lookup.
Abstract: Quantitative reasoning is a hallmark of intelligence; we ask whether it rests on an abstract, language-independent magnitude representation inside LLMs. We probe residual-stream activations for numbers presented as digits, English words, and words in three other languages, and fit a low-dimensional magnitude manifold. We test (i) whether a single manifold predicts magnitude across all notations/languages (shared code) versus separate per-notation codes, (ii) whether distances on the manifold obey magnitude relations (ordering, approximate ratio structure), and (iii) whether perturbing a number's position along the manifold causally shifts arithmetic outputs by the predicted amount. We relate per-model manifold fidelity (how cleanly magnitude is linearly recoverable and ordered) to arithmetic and estimation accuracy across model sizes. We predict a shared cross-notation, cross-lingual magnitude subspace whose geometric fidelity tracks quantitative-reasoning skill, and that causal edits along it move answers predictably. Demonstrating a unified, causal number line beneath diverse linguistic surfaces would show that quantitative intelligence in LLMs is grounded in an abstract magnitude representation rather than token-level pattern matching, explain cross-notation transfer, and provide a concrete measure linking representational geometry to reasoning competence.
Experiments: Stimuli: integers 0-1000 as digits, English words, and words in Spanish, Chinese, Hindi; plus arithmetic prompts.
Extract residual activations at the number token across layers for Llama-3-8B/70B, Qwen2.5, Pythia sizes.
Fit magnitude manifold (PCA + probe); test cross-notation/cross-lingual generalization of a single magnitude probe.
Geometry tests: ordering accuracy along principal axis; check approximate ratio/log structure.
Causal edit: shift a number's manifold coordinate by delta and measure change in emitted arithmetic result.
Fidelity-vs-skill: correlate per-model manifold linear-recoverability with arithmetic/estimation accuracy across sizes.
Metrics: cross-notation probe transfer accuracy, ordering fidelity, causal-edit predicted-vs-actual shift, fidelity-accuracy correlation.
Control: non-numeric tokens should not lie on the manifold; scrambled-label probe baseline.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Digit tokenization can fragment numbers, complicating position selection and manifold fitting.
Probes may capture token identity rather than abstract magnitude despite cross-notation tests.
The manifold may be piecewise (per range) rather than globally continuous.
Causal edits may destabilize computation and produce nonlinear effects.
Cross-lingual number words vary in tokenization, confounding comparisons.
